description: Also known as common leaf spot, it is a prevalent fungal disease affecting strawberry foliage, significantly reducing photosynthetic capability when severe.
symptoms: Circular, deep purple spots on the upper leaf surface.
Spots enlarge to about 1/4 inch in diameter with centers turning grayish-white on older leaves and light brown on young leaves.
A definite reddish-purple to rusty-brown border surrounds the leaf spots.
Black fungal fruiting bodies visible in the light-colored centers of older lesions.
Superficial black spots about 1/4 inch in diameter forming on ripe fruit around groups of seeds under moist conditions.
favorable_conditions: Wet weather conditions.
Frequent prolonged periods of leaf wetness.
spread: Overwintering spores inside debris of infected leaves and plants.
prevention: Select and plant resistant strawberry cultivars.
Use clean, certified disease-free planting material.
integrated_management: Remove infected leaves and old leaf debris from the field to reduce overwintering inoculum.
Apply mulch to prevent soil and water splash onto foliage.
Increase plant spacing to improve air circulation and encourage rapid leaf drying.
treatment: Apply protective fungicides if the disease becomes severe and weather conditions favor spread.
safety_notes: Follow fungicide label instructions regarding personal protective equipment (PPE) and restricted-entry intervals (REI).

description: Strawberry plants exhibiting normal physiological development, free from macroscopic symptoms or signs of infectious disease, pathogen colonization, or nutrient deficiencies.
favorable_conditions: Optimal daytime temperatures between 60°F and 80°F.
Well-drained soils with balanced nutrient profiles.
Adequate spacing ensuring low canopy humidity and rapid drying.
prevention: Utilizing drip irrigation instead of overhead systems to prevent canopy wetness.
integrated_management: Regular scouting of fields to monitor for early signs of pests or stressors.
Maintaining good sanitation by removing weeds and plant debris.

sources.title: Integrated Pest Management for Strawberries
sources.organization: University of California Statewide IPM Program

description: A foliar phase of powdery mildew caused by an obligate fungal parasite that thrives in high-humidity microclimates, significantly causing leaf curling and tissue discoloration.
symptoms: Small white patches of fungal mycelium growing on the lower leaf surface.
Dense powdery white appearance on the underside of leaves as mycelial growth expands.
Irregular yellow or reddish-brown spots developing on the lower leaf surface and breaking through to the upper surface in certain cultivars.
Upward curling of the edges of heavily infected leaves.
Production of small round chasmothecia (cleistothecia) on leaf undersides, changing from white to black as they mature.
favorable_conditions: Moderate to high relative humidity.
Temperatures between 60°F and 80°F.
Protected culture environments such as greenhouses or plastic tunnels where dry conditions coincide with high humidity.
spread: Introduction of infected, living green transplants from nursery operations.
prevention: Utilize cultivars exhibiting higher degrees of genetic resistance.
integrated_management: Regularly survey fields with susceptible cultivars early in the growing season.
Avoid excess shading and maintain proper plant densities to mitigate high-humidity pockets within the plant canopy.
treatment: Apply protective fungicides, such as elemental sulfur, preventively or at the first structural sign of the disease.
Rotate systemic fungicides (e.g., pyraclostrobin + fluxapyroxad, fluopyram, or penthiopyrad) to avoid the development of pathogen resistance.
safety_notes: Free water from rain, heavy dew, and overhead irrigation actively inhibits this specific fungus.
Adhere strictly to chemical rotation guidelines due to high baseline risks of fungicide resistance.

description: A devastating, globally distributed fungal disease capable of infecting almost all plant tissues, causing severe pre- and post-harvest fruit decay and yield losses exceeding 50%.
symptoms: Infected fruit tissues turn light to medium brown in color.
Development of a velvety, grayish-colored mass of fungal mycelium and conidia over infected surfaces under high humidity.
Infections under low humidity present as brown, shriveled, and leathery tissue without visible sporulation.
Small brown lesions appearing on the berry, frequently initiating directly beneath the calyx.
Mummification of heavily diseased fruit.
favorable_conditions: Cool weather combined with frequent rainfall or free water during the flowering and fruiting periods.
High relative humidity within dense plant canopies.
spread: Microscopic asexual spores (conidia) dispersed by wind and water splash.
Mycelium and sclerotia overwintering in plant detritus, dead leaves, and alternative weed hosts.
prevention: Select cultivars with open canopy architecture to improve ventilation.
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization that promotes overly dense foliar growth.
integrated_management: Strict sanitation, including the physical removal and destruction of infected or senescing plant tissue and mummified berries.
Utilize drip irrigation rather than overhead systems to minimize canopy wetness.
Apply straw mulch to create a physical barrier between the soil debris and developing clusters.
treatment: Apply targeted protectant and systemic fungicides during the critical bloom period when flowers are highly susceptible.
Utilize predictive tools like the Strawberry Advisory System (StAS) to optimize spray timing based on leaf wetness and temperature.
safety_notes: Latent infections can establish during bloom and remain completely dormant until fruit sugar content increases during ripening, leading to sudden post-harvest rot.

description: The only major bacterial disease affecting strawberries, primarily inducing foliar damage but capable of causing system-wide collapse and severe export quarantine issues.
symptoms: Tiny, water-soaked lesions appearing on the lower leaf surface, strictly delimited by small veins.
Lesions appear angular, translucent, and yellow to pale green when held up to a light source.
Lesions appear dark green and opaque when viewed from above under reflected light.
A slimy white film or milky bacterial exudate oozing from spots under wet conditions.
Exudate dries into a scaly film, producing white flakes that can be scraped off the leaf.
Lesions merge over time, appearing on upper leaf surfaces as reddish-brown necrotic areas.
Ragged leaf margins as dead tissue dries out and breaks off.
favorable_conditions: Cool to moderate daytime temperatures (65°F to 70°F) coupled with cold nighttime temperatures near freezing.
Wet conditions driven by rain, heavy dew, or overhead irrigation.
Vigorously growing, young vegetative tissue.
spread: Splashing rain and overhead irrigation water transferring bacterial cells.
Introduction into clean fields via infected systemic transplants.
Field workers handling plants when the foliage is physically wet.
prevention: Exclusively use certified, disease-free transplants, as no commercially available varieties possess full resistance.
Enforce strict sanitation protocols for tools and footwear between fields.
integrated_management: Avoid the use of overhead irrigation to minimize water splash.
Increase plant spacing to accelerate canopy drying.
Physically remove infected foliage if operating on a manageable scale.
Implement crop rotation to avoid planting into infested residue.
treatment: Copper-containing compounds are registered for use but offer limited efficacy and can cause direct phytotoxicity with repeated applications.
safety_notes: The bacterium is host-specific to strawberry and does not survive free-living in the soil without host debris, though it can survive inside buried debris for long periods.
Systemic movement into crowns can cause sudden vascular collapse and plant death.

description: A destructive disease complex of strawberry flowers caused by bacterial or fungal agents, leading to direct flower abortion, malformed fruit development, or latent fruit infections.
pathogen: Botrytis cinerea or Xanthomonas fragariae or Cladosporium cladosporioides
symptoms: Bacterial (X. fragariae) symptoms show dark green, water-soaked lesions on sepals under reflected light, appearing translucent under transmitted light.
Water-soaking of the base of the calyx extending rapidly into the pedicel, causing necrosis.
Fungal (C. cladosporioides) infections turn anthers black, covered with olivaceous green-gray sporulation.
Fungal (B. cinerea) symptoms cause rapid browning and dry rotting of petals, pistils, and reproductive organs within days of opening.
Girdling and collapse of the pedicel, leading to complete blighting of the attached flower cluster.
favorable_conditions: Extended periods of cool, wet weather coinciding exactly with open blossoms.
High relative humidity within the plant canopy during spring bloom.
spread: Water splash from rain or overhead irrigation dispersing pathogens onto open flower parts.
Wind dissemination of fungal conidia across planting rows.
prevention: Source certified disease-free planting material to prevent bringing bacterial blighters into fields.
Select production sites with good air drainage.
integrated_management: Strict avoidance of overhead irrigation during the flowering window.
Maintain rigorous weed control to eliminate microclimatic humidity and alternative hosts.
treatment: Apply protective fungicides targeted for Botrytis at early bloom (pre-bloom through fruit set).
For bacterial agents, copper sprays may be applied early if labeled, but carry risks of flower phytotoxicity.
safety_notes: Simultaneous co-infection of flowers by both bacterial and fungal pathogens can accelerate the severity of tissue necrosis and complete flower cluster abortion.

description: The fruit-infecting phase of powdery mildew, which colonizes floral organs and both immature and mature fruit, leading to significant downgrading of fruit quality and marketable yield.
symptoms: Fungal colonization of flowers leading to aborted, misshapen, or malformed fruit development.
White, fuzzy mycelial growth covering the achenes (seeds) on the surface of older fruit.
Loss of fruit gloss, drying out of the fruit surface, and severe reduction in fresh-market visual quality.
favorable_conditions: Moderate to high humidity combined with warm daytime temperatures (60°F to 80°F).
Absence of free liquid water on the fruit surface, making covered or greenhouse cultures highly vulnerable.
spread: Wind-blown conidia moving from infected foliar canopies onto newly developing fruit structures.
prevention: Plant cultivars known to express fruit-phase resistance to powdery mildew.
integrated_management: Perform intensive early-season scouting of leaves to manage the disease before fruit formation occurs.
Ensure proper plant row orientation to allow maximum sunlight penetration into the fruiting zone.
treatment: Apply protective elemental sulfur sprays early in the season before visible fruit symptoms occur.
Utilize systemic fungicides like pyraclostrobin + fluxapyroxad or fluopyram, adhering to pre-harvest intervals (PHI).
safety_notes: Because the fruit phase is highly difficult to suppress once established on the achenes, management must focus entirely on preventing vegetative populations from building up.

description: One of the most destructive warm-weather diseases impacting strawberry production, causing distinct firm, sunken dark rot lesions directly on green and ripening fruit.
symptoms: Small (1/16 to 1/8 inch), hard, sunken, dark brown or black lesions on immature green fruit.
Larger (1/8 to 1/2 inch), circular, firm, sunken tan-to-dark brown lesions on ripening fruit.
Under warm, humid, or wet weather, lesions produce a sticky, light orange, salmon, or pink mucilaginous mass of millions of spores.
Under completely dry conditions, infected fruit becomes deeply sunken, blackens, and dries up completely into a mummified berry.
Developing fruit remains small, hard, and misshapen if infection occurs immediately post-pollination.
favorable_conditions: Unusually warm weather combined with frequent rainfall or overhead irrigation.
Optimum temperatures around 68°F (20°C) specifically for fruit infection by C. acutatum.
Prolonged leaf and fruit wetness durations.
spread: Introduction of latent, entirely asymptomatic infections on nursery runner plants and plugs.
Water splash from wind-driven rain or overhead irrigation moving conidia from leaves to fruit.
Contaminated farm equipment, harvesters, and field workers moving through rows, especially when plants are wet.
prevention: Source transplants from certified micropropagated pathogen-free programs.
Utilize less susceptible cultivars (e.g., 'Sweet Charlie' or 'Bish') where regionally appropriate.
integrated_management: Strictly avoid overhead irrigation; implement drip irrigation systems.
Apply clean straw mulch to minimize the springboard effect of water droplets on plastic mulch.
Enforce strict field sanitation: cull infected plants and remove all mummified fruit.
Always work fields from clean areas to infected areas, picking infested zones last to limit mechanical transfer.
Rotate out of strawberries for at least 2 to 3 years to let soil inoculum loads decline.
treatment: Apply protective fungicides (e.g., captan) starting pre-bloom and continuing through harvest.
Use systemic strobilurin fungicides (e.g., azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin) or combination products during high-risk periods, unless pathogen resistance is confirmed.
Time sprays precisely using data-driven web tools like the Strawberry Advisory System (StAS).
safety_notes: A single infected berry can produce hundreds of thousands of conidia, causing explosive field epidemics if mismanaged.
Do not apply captan in direct combination with, immediately before, or closely following oil sprays due to phytotoxicity risks.
